title: His First GMC 2500 Gave This Truck Collector a Lifelong Quest

body_markdown:
For decades now, John Mullen has had a 1967-72 GM “Action Line” pickup truck in his life. Or several.


“As a kid, I found a GMC 2500, a Camper Special, with four-wheel drive. When I turned 16, I took out a loan for $2000 and bought it,” Mullen recounted. “That was my first work truck. I cut firewood, and hauled it in the truck for a whole year.


“When I turned 17, me and three of my buddies jumped in it and drove to Texas. In the Eighties, there was no work in upstate New York. We drove it down there and all got jobs building houses. We pretty much lived in that truck for months: We put a mattress in the back and slept in it before we got an apartment.”


John Mullen is happiest behind the wheel of his 1972 GMC 2500 Sierra Grande pickup—identical to his first-ever truck, which he bought at age 16.


DW Burnett


The long-bed Custom Camper package was rare in 1972, and survivors are highly prized today.


DW Burnett


A life of hard work has panned out for Mullen. He now runs a construction company based in New York’s Hudson Valley, which employs 80 people year-round (and up to 110 in the summer). Among other types of building jobs, it installs energy infrastructure that includes natural-gas pipelines and high-voltage electrical cables.


Mullen has lived in the Catskills since he was a boy; now he “can’t imagine living anywhere else.”


DW Burnett


As Mullen tells it, much of that work was enabled by a series of new and used GMC and Chevrolet trucks. As his company grew, he added more buildings for vehicle storage—and did the same on the Catskill Mountains farm where he lives. There, two wide timber garages each hold up to eight vehicles, with more than a dozen others of all kinds parked outside. They’re mostly GM trucks from the 1960s and 1970s, but a 1960s Dodge Power Wagon appears too.


A successful contractor, Mullen built multiple garages for his growing collection—here, lined up for photographs.


DW Burnett


## His First Love


In the end, Mullen couldn’t keep the truck he bought back in 1980. He had to sell it to a friend, who scrapped it once upstate New York road salt took its toll. “That was just what you did in the Eighties,” he shrugged. But he never forgot it—and the impact of that first GMC truck would last a lifetime.


Why is Mullen so attracted to these specific trucks? He paused for a minute to think.


DW Burnett


“I just fell in love with them. I learned how to drive on a ’68 GMC C-10, with a three-on-the-tree. There were so many of them, then. And when you’re a young kid, you just pay attention to every detail—‘cause you had to do that, to fix it constantly.”


It took years of hard work before Mullen had the stability and resources in the mid-1990s to return to his first truck love. Over the 30 years that followed, his collection expanded as other models and versions became available. (He ended up selling the first “new” one he bought when he found better, lower-mileage trucks.)


The luxury aspect of the Sierra Grande package extended to wood-grain trim and this rare badge.


DW Burnett


Patterned upholstery, wood-grain trim, automatic, A/C, power steering … it all makes Mullen’s 2500 Camper Special an early ancestor of today’s GMC Denali luxury trim.


DW Burnett


Ten years ago, he finally located an exact duplicate of his very first truck. It came all the way from Georgia, but it’s a rare 1972 GMC 2500 Camper Special with the Sierra Grande trim package. The Camper Special was a long-bed model with built-in dual gas tanks, filled via flaps on the forward outside panels of the bed. Meanwhile, the Sierra Grande option includes not only his original pickup’s two-tone green-and-white paint, but the checked upholstery pattern. This one has two outright luxuries for trucks of that era: an automatic transmission and air conditioning.


All but one of John Mullen’s trucks now have 350-cubic-inch V-8s, but low rear-axle ratios mean they can take a while to get up to speed.


DW Burnett


Until recently, he also had a Longhorn model of the same vintage, with an extra-long 8-foot, 6-inch bed length to accommodate the largest slide-in campers. His niece now drives that one. But because the green Camper Special is the same model truck on which he learned to drive, Mullen uses it locally when he’s not in a company work rig. It’s still only racked up 40,000 miles over 50-plus years. The rest of the fleet is used regularly as well.


## All About the Fire Companies


Mullen admitted he has a specific way to find rust-free trucks half a century old, with very low original mileages. (His trucks ranged from 12,000 to 40,000 miles when he bought them.) “Instead of watching the TV news, I go through the municipal auctions. I do that for heavy equipment, too, ‘cause I have 150 trucks and pieces of other equipment on the road.”


His secret is that diligent attention to local fire-company auctions has really paid off, since most fire companies put surplus equipment up for auction to get the best price. Half of the eight trucks featured in this article came from local fire departments.


The interior of Mullen’s 1972 Chevrolet C/20 shows just how basic trucks were half a century ago. From a local fire company, it now has 18,000 original miles.


DW Burnett


Not that it’s always smooth sailing. In 2010, Mullen put in a bid on a 1972 Chevy C/20 with 18,000 original miles offered by a village fire company just 35 miles north of his town. He knew his bid was the highest. But that wasn’t the end of the story: “They had to do a background check, to make sure I was going to be a good home.” He didn’t learn if they’d accepted him as the new owner for two long months. “It was agonizing,” he admits. In the end, he got the truck, which still sports its original red paint—though he had the upper body sprayed white for the factory two-tone look.


When Mullen was 11 or 12, the house his family lived in caught fire and burned. A local fire company responded, and he always remembered the first truck to arrive on the scene. It’s a point of pride for him that when that 1974 International fire truck was deemed surplus and put up for sale, he could buy and preserve it as a way of saying thanks.


## Some Original, Some Customized


Mullen’s not a purist with his trucks, and the green-and-white Camper Special is now as close as he can make it to his first truck—including a 2-inch lift kit and larger chrome wheels with knobbier tires. Several of the trucks have that same lift and similar wheels. All but one came with, or later received, 350 small-block V-8s. Some have also gained rooftop fire-truck lights.


Mullen is fond of fire-company accessories; several of his trucks sport roof lights like these. Some are original, some have been added.


DW Burnett


More fire-company gear: a manually pivoting spotlight to light emergency scenes.


DW Burnett


Mullen’s 1968 C/20, originally a pumper truck, has no Park setting for its 2-speed TurboHydro automatic; a mechanical brake lock serves that purpose instead.


DW Burnett


Unlike many trucks today, when you open the hood of a ‘60s or ‘70s pickup, you can actually see the engine.


DW Burnett


A select few remain in their stock condition. His red 1969 Chevy C/20 had been a fire truck in another nearby town less than 50 miles south. The fire department ordered it new as a Stepside, and fitted a pumper into the narrow bed, which he removed and kept. At only 21,000 miles, it’s presently titled as a farm truck—making it one of two vehicles in the group he couldn’t let us drive on public roads.


This 1969 Chevy C/20 Stepside also came from a local fire company; with only 21,000 original miles, it’s presently licensed as a farm truck.


DW Burnett


A faded red-brown 1972 GMC 1000 Custom came from Texas with a mere 14,000 miles. The owner had used it for backwoods camping, but when Mullen removed the shell and then pulled out the carpet that lined the bed, he found the bed itself was practically mint. That one has its original 250 cubic-inch inline-six, paired to a column-shift three-speed transmission. It even sports the original GMC hubcaps; he has added only the red roof spotlights from a fire truck.


Because Mullen uses his 1971 Chevy Suburban—the three-door model—for long trips, he added insulation to quiet this 14K-mile Vermont fire-company crew truck.


DW Burnett


Mullen’s appreciation of GM’s 1967-72 “Action Line” truck design isn’t limited to the pickup models. He also has a 1971 Chevy Suburban, from a Vermont fire company that sold it with just 14,000 miles. It’s a seldom-seen three-door example, a design that ran only from 1967 through 1972, after which the company added a fourth door on the left-hand side. As his first Suburban, Mullen treated the truck to a careful, high-quality paint job inside and out from local shop Starr Automotive. He also added sound deadening to make the large metal box on wheels more usable on road trips. It too has the characteristic 2-inch lift kit, along with fire-truck spotlights.


Mullen flew to Chicago and back in a day to nail down this 1971 GMC Jimmy in Medium Bronze Iridescent; after mechanical refurbishment, he uses it regularly.


DW Burnett


Then there’s the 1972 GMC Jimmy, in its original root beer color combo. This one he found in Chicago, again with virtually no rust—and an automatic. Mullen wanted the truck badly enough to take a day off from work, fly to Chicago, inspect it, buy it, and fly back that evening. The Jimmy arrived on a truck in a few weeks, to be rebuilt by his school buddy and mechanic Scott Spencer, who he just calls “the C20 guy.”


DW Burnett


## Using Them Regularly and Giving Back


The vehicles are all driven regularly, and Mullen is generous with his fleet. They’re often loaned to relatives, friends, employees, and neighbors. They mostly live at the farm, can often be found at his company, and are seen regularly on country roads all over the Catskills. Among the workers closest to the trucks and most proud of them are RJ Nerone and Jason Podmayersky, who won our thanks for helping to wrangle eight trucks over a photo shoot that ran from 9 a.m. to 6:30 p.m.


Yet another fire-company truck, in this case from outside Buffalo, Mullen’s 1971 GMC 2500 got a frame-off restoration, his characteristic 2-inch lift, and spotlights.


DW Burnett


In a longer and more philosophical discussion about trucks and life, Mullen said he’s been successful, and his goal is to give back to his town and his community. The Andrew Mullen Memorial Trout Fishing Derby, held in May each year, invites local kids and families—seemingly hundreds of them—to compete for the largest fish they can catch in the farm’s pond. (Sure, maybe he stocks it the week before, but still.) There’s a pancake breakfast, hot dogs and hamburgers, music, door prizes galore, and a real spirit of small-town community among families, some who’ve known each other for generations.


The important part: The event has raised $350,000 since it started, given as scholarships to a total of 170 local high-school graduates accepted to trade schools, apprenticeships, and colleges. This June alone, Mullen awarded 29 graduating seniors $100 to $2500 in scholarships.


The trucks are on prominent display at the derby, with the farm’s horses, goats, chickens, and a pair of donkeys wandering unfazed through the event. Off to the side of the truck garages, Mullen also has C-30s (the larger and heavier-duty version of the truck from the same era)—and several pieces of heavier equipment, as well.


Mullen built the barn, the pond, and everything else on his farm; what you don’t see are the garages for eight GMC and Chevy trucks, including the Suburban.


DW Burnett


Despite the baleful look, the donkeys are quite used to the noise of the old trucks by now—as are the goats, the sheep, and various other animals.


DW Burnett


This shot shows five-eighths of Mullen’s current stable of Chevy and GMC trucks—but he has another eight down at company headquarters. Who knows, there may be more coming…


DW Burnett


Meanwhile, he’s not quite done with the collection. Toward the end of our day of driving and photographing, he mentioned both a 1952 Diamond Reo tow truck and another eight GMC and Chevrolet models, all waiting their turn down at the company shop. Some new C-10s and C-20s may soon join their siblings at the farm. Once they arrive, you’ll see them on the roads of the Catskill Mountains. And if you’re lucky, John Mullen will be behind the wheel … with a big grin.
